title: tbody
description: Grouping a table's main data rows, and using multiple tbody sections.
subject: html
html:
The <tbody> element groups a table's main data rows — separate from its header (<thead>) and footer (<tfoot>) sections.

Syntax

<tbody>
    <tr><td>Data row</td></tr>
</tbody>

Basic Example

<table>
    <thead>
        <tr><th>Name</th><th>Score</th></tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr><td>Aman</td><td>92</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Priya</td><td>85</td></tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

Browser output: visually indistinguishable from a table with no explicit sections at all — <tbody>'s benefit is structural and scriptable, not a default visual change.

How It Works

Unlike <thead> and <tfoot> (each allowed only once), a table can technically contain multiple <tbody> sections — useful for grouping logically distinct blocks of rows within one table, though most tables only need one.

Important Attributes

AttributePurpose
— none special —Only universal global attributes apply

Real-World Example

<table>
    <thead><tr><th>Item</th><th>Qty</th></tr></thead>

    <tbody>
        <tr><td>Keyboard</td><td>10</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Mouse</td><td>10</td></tr>
    </tbody>

    <tbody>
        <tr><td>Monitor</td><td>5</td></tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

Two separate <tbody> groups — perhaps representing two different supplier shipments within the same overall inventory table, each independently stylable via CSS.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming a table always needs an explicit <tbody> to work — it renders fine without one, but the browser silently inserts an implied <tbody> for you anyway, so writing it explicitly is simply clearer
  • Forgetting that multiple <tbody> elements are allowed and useful for logically grouping rows

Best Practices

  • Always write <tbody> explicitly for clarity, even though the browser would imply one
  • Use multiple <tbody> sections when a table genuinely has distinct logical groups of rows

Accessibility Considerations

Clear sectioning helps both scripting and, indirectly, assistive technology tools that rely on well-structured markup to summarize or navigate a large table.

SEO Considerations

No direct ranking effect.

Browser & Modern HTML Notes

Browsers have always implicitly wrapped bare rows in a <tbody> even when you don't write one — a detail worth knowing when inspecting a page's rendered DOM and seeing a <tbody> you never typed.

Mini Practice

  1. Add explicit <thead> and <tbody> to a table that currently has none.
  2. Split a 6-row table into two <tbody> groups of 3 rows each, based on a logical grouping.
